convoLines.text: "Pantry's thin and getting thinner. Forage with me tomorrow? I know the meadow edge, west of the creek."
"I did the count twice. The count doesn't change. Nobody's worked the meadow edge, west of the creek in days. We'll fill packs before dark."
Your partner is inside the Haven hall. Go through the door to meet them.
"Sorry — I shouldn't load that on you. What's up?"
"There's still the matter of the ambush of Rahim. Nobody's settled it."
Done — their story has a crack in it now.
"Okay, that's my quota of socializing."
They glance at the fire, then back. The quiet doesn't seem to bother them.
"...Think about it? I'll be around."
"I can't reach this properly. Could you take a look?"
"It's getting worse, not better. If it festers I'm no good to anyone — can't haul, can't hunt, can't watch. Just clean it out and wrap it tight."
Move next to them, on the same side of the Haven door, to help.
"Forget I said anything. What did you want?"
"There's still the matter of the ambush of Rahim. Nobody's settled it."
There — the story splits again. You mark the spot.
They fill the quiet. "Anyway — where was I?"
Their voice loosens. The guardedness thins.
"Right. I get it." A beat — and then the subject is closed. They won't raise it again.
The ground remembers.
Names, named.
You watch who eats with whom, who laughs a little too loud at whose jokes. Nothing solid. Keep looking.
"Go. But sit with what I said."
"Okay. I'll manage on my own."
"Good day, huh? Almost feels normal."
"Walk with me? I want another pair of eyes on something."
It's quiet at the tree line. Hank doesn't say much. Sometimes that's the whole point.
"Anyway." A small smile.
"Still on cheer."
"Someone should watch your back. Might as well be me."
"I should go. You know where to find me."
You say nothing. Neither do they, for a while — and it's fine.
"...Think about it? I'll be around."
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
«Vizuri uwepo hapa. Kweli.» "Sorry?" — they grin, proud of the one English they know.
«Ndiyo, ndiyo, hasa.» They nod back, slowly.
«Sitaisahau wema huu.» (you catch 'wema' — kindness) A grin breaks through, quick and warm.
«Kila kitu kitakuwa sawa.» (you catch 'sawa' — okay) You tap your chest, then theirs. Us. They nod, emphatic.
You listen hard, watching their mouth shape the words. «Una chakula? Chochote?» (you catch 'chakula' — food)
Wanjiru laughs — with you, mostly. "Good try! Again — Ndiyo, ndiyo, hasa.." They walk you through it, patient as sunrise.
They hear the warmth in it. They're not ready to let it in.
"Sure. I'll be around."
"This was good." They mean it.
People need to know someone's got a plan. Even if the plan is 'we'll figure it out.'
"There's still the matter of the murder of Rahim. Nobody's settled it."
Another crack. The telling doesn't hold together anymore.
The ground remembers.
Names, named.
You watch who eats with whom, who laughs a little too loud at whose jokes. Nothing solid. Keep looking.
The moot is called. The fire gets built up.
You say nothing. The silence sits at the fire with everyone else.
"Alright — I should get back to it."
A comfortable quiet settles. They smile a little, and let it be.
"...Think about it? I'll be around."
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
«Habari! Wewe... jina lako nani?» (you catch 'Habari' — hello)
The moot is called. The fire gets built up.
Counted.
«Hasa hivyo. Kama ulivyosema.» (Exactly so. As you said. — you're fairly sure) They nod back, slowly. "Hello?"
«Wewe ni mtu mwema.» (You are a good person. — you're fairly sure) A grin breaks through, quick and warm.
«Asante kwa kuwa hapa.» (Thanks for being here. — you're fairly sure) You tap your chest, then theirs. Us. They nod, emphatic.
You listen hard, watching their mouth shape the words. «Wewe ndiye... kiongozi hapa?» (Are you... the leader here? — you're fairly sure)
They glance toward their own thoughts; the exchange is winding down.
You say nothing. Neither do they, for a while — and it's fine.
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
«Hei... unasema Kiswahili? Hapana? ...lahaula.» (Hey... you speak Swahili? No? ...oh dear. — you're fairly sure) "Sorry?" — they grin, proud of the one English they know.
«Ndiyo, uko sahihi.» (Yes, you're correct. — you're fairly sure) They nod back, slowly.
«Sitaisahau wema huu.» (I will not forget this kindness. — you're fairly sure) A grin breaks through, quick and warm.
«Kila kitu kitakuwa sawa.» (Everything will be okay. — you're fairly sure) You tap your chest, then theirs. Us. They nod, emphatic.
You listen hard, watching their mouth shape the words. «Huku watu hulala wapi? Ni salama?» (Here where do people sleep? Is it safe? — you're fairly sure)
"Right. Go on, then."
"This was good." They mean it.
"Do you ever just need to be alone? Like, really alone?"
"I get it. Solitude's a resource too. Scarcer than food, some days."
"Hah. I go to the treeline edge and count my breaths. Ten of them. That's my alone. Then I come back — alone is a luxury, and also a little bit a lie."
"Still on needing to be alone."
"Not right now. I've got my own things to handle."
"Sorry — I shouldn't load that on you. What's up?"
"The whole fire was arguing about Speedbump last night — what to even CALL it. 'The Big Thing' got shouted down. What's your vote?"
"Take your time."
You show them Dandelion — where it grows, how to tell it apart. They nod slowly, committing it to memory. "Good to know. Really good to know."
"Names are for when it's dead or known. Right now it's neither, so I tend the fire without being asked instead."
"Alright, duty calls. This was a good pause."
You say nothing. Neither do they, for a while — and it's fine.
"Good talk. I feel like I know you a little better now."
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
"Can I tell you something? I stole medicine from the stash once and never confessed."
"Come see what I found. You won't believe it."
It's quiet at the hollow. Zoe doesn't say much. Sometimes that's the whole point.
"This one — Mahua. Leaf, stem, smell. You won't forget it now."
Their eyes do the math before their mouth does. You can see the calculation happening.
"You know what, fair." Zoe nods slowly. "I can see how that looked. But here's the thing..." And the thing is mundane, and verifiable, and fine.
"So." They look at the fire for a moment.
"So, uh — Still on their secret."
A warmth settles over the conversation — they lean in a little.
"...Sorry, lost my train of thought."
"...Anyway. What did you want to ask? Just... be straight with me."
"I dreamed Tashi was still here. Woke up angry at the dream. Stupid."
You show them Dandelion — where it grows, how to tell it apart. "Huh." They turn it over in their mind. "I'll remember that one."
"I keep turning over the last thing Tashi said to me. I can't tell if I'm remembering it right, and that's somehow the worst part."
"Alright — I should get back to it."
You say nothing. Neither do they, for a while — and it's fine.
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
"This cut — I can't clean it properly one-handed. Could you clean it out for me? Please."
"It's getting worse, not better. If it festers I'm no good to anyone — can't haul, can't hunt, can't watch. Just clean it out and wrap it tight."
Move next to them, on the same side of the Haven door, to help.
"Sorry — I shouldn't load that on you. What's up?"
"There's more, but that's for another fire."
"Tashi is gone and the world just... continues. That's the part I can't stand."
"Okay. Yeah. I trust you."
"Okay I really have to move now or I'll explode — talk soon!"
A comfortable quiet settles. They smile a little, and let it be.
"...Think about it? I'll be around."
"This was good." They mean it.

d54: 🌙 Raid — Emberhold came in the night from the southwest. They carried off ~1200 kcal from the pantry. Nobody's dead, but the message is clear: the ground is theirs too, and they're done asking. (Trus
